sections.title: How does the Recessed lighting calculator work?
sections.html:
The Recessed lighting calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports rows of lighting fixtures in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case; then you type in the outer row offset (aₒ), the row spacing (ai), the outer column offset (bₒ) and the column spacing (bi).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Recessed lighting calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Rows of lighting fixtures=(1 ÷ 2) × surface length (A) ÷ outer row offset (aₒ)
Rows of lighting fixtures=surface length (A) ÷ row spacing (ai)
Columns of lighting fixtures=(1 ÷ 2) × surface width (B) ÷ outer column offset (bₒ)
Columns of lighting fixtures=surface width (B) ÷ column spacing (bi)
Centered lighting's vertical offset (yₒ)=surface length (A) ÷ rows of lighting fixtures
Centered lightings' spacing (yi)=surface length (A) ÷ rows of lighting fixtures

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Surface length (A) = 30 m, Columns of lighting fixtures set to 1, Rows of lighting fixtures set to 1 and Outer row offset (aₒ) = 30 cm. The calculator returns Row spacing (ai) = 30 cm, Centered lighting's vertical offset (yₒ) = 30 cm and Centered lightings' spacing (yi) = 30 cm.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Row spacing (ai) = 30 cm, Centered lighting's vertical offset (yₒ) = 30 cm and Centered lightings' spacing (yi) = 30 cm should be roughly the size you expected from Surface length (A) = 30 m and Columns of lighting fixtures set to 1.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Recessed lighting calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the outer row offset, the row spacing and the outer column offset — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Recessed lighting calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns rows of lighting fixtures, derived from the outer row offset, the row spacing and the outer column offset. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Recessed lighting calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the outer row offset, the row spacing, the outer column offset and the column spacing, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter surface length (A) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Surface length (A) opens in meters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (3 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Row spacing (ai) = 30 cm. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Recessed lighting calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
